source_text: ὠμὸν οὐκ ἔχοντα καὶ ἀπηχθημένον. Διεπύθου δέ που τὸν ἐν ἁγνείαις ἐπὶ τὴν σωτήριον τροφὴν, ὥσπερ ἰδίαν ὀνομάζοντος τοῦ Χριστοῦ καὶ λέγοντος τοῖς ἁγίοις μαθηταῖς· «Ἐγὼ βρῶσιν ἔχω φαγεῖν, ἣν ὑμεῖς οὐκ οἴδατε.» Διαμέμνησο δὲ ὅτι καὶ καταθύεσθαι μὲν ἐκέλευε τὸν ἀμνὸν, εἰς τύπον Χριστοῦ, προσενομοθέτει δὲ λέγων· «Οὐ φάγεσθε ἀπ' αὐτῶν ὠμὸν, οὐδὲ ἑψημένον ἐν ὕδατι, ἀλλ' ἢ ὀπτὰ πυρί·» τὸ ἀπαράδεκτον, οἶμαί που, καὶ τὸ οἱονείπως εἰς πέψιν οὐκ εὐχερὲς, ὠμὸν εἶναι λέγων. Χρῆναι δὴ οὖν ἄρα φησὶν ἑφθὸν λαμβάνεσθαι τὸν βραχίονα· τοῦ ἀνέφθου σημαίνοντος τὸ μήτε ἡδὺ, μήτε βρώσιμον, ταύτῃτοι καὶ ἀπαράδεκτον. {ΠΑΛΛ.} Ὡς ἰσχνὸς ἄγαν καὶ ἀληθὴς ὁ λόγος. {ΚΥΡ.} Ἀποδοτέον οὖν ἄρα τὰς ὁμολογίας Θεῷ, καὶ ἅπερ ἂν εὔξαιτό τις, διαπεραινέτω μελλήσας οὐδὲν, ὡς τό τοι μὴ δρᾷν τὰ τοιάδε γοργῶς, τῶν ὅτι μάλιστα δεινῶν καὶ σφαλερωτάτων φαίην ἂν ἔγωγε, καὶ αὐτὸ δὲ τὸ Γράμμα τὸ ἱερόν. Εἰ γὰρ εἶναι λογιούμεθα φρονοῦντες ὀρθῶς τῶν ἄγαν ἐκτοπωτάτων, τὸ ψευδοεπείας ἁλῶναι γραφῇ, πῶς οὐκ ἂν γένοιτο τῶν λίαν αἰσχρῶν, ὁμολογῆσαι μέν τι καὶ ὑποσχέσθαι Θεῷ, ψεύσασθαι δὲ μετὰ τοῦτο τὴν ὑπόσχεσιν; Παντὸς μὲν οὖν εὐξαμένου καὶ μελλήσαντος, καὶ γοῦν καὶ εἰσάπαν ἀναδυομένου τὴν ἔκτισιν, καταγράφει τὴν ἁμαρτίαν. Ἀνίησι δὲ τῶν αἰτιαμάτων τοὺς ἔχοντας μὲν παντελῶς ἴδιον οὐδὲν, δεσμῷ δὲ ὥσπερ ἀναγκαίῳ κατεζευγμένους, καὶ ὑφ' ἑτέρου πράττοντας χεῖρα. Γέγραπται δὲ οὕτως ἐν τοῖς Ἀριθμοῖς· «Καὶ ἐλάλησε Μωσῆς πρὸς τοὺς ἄρχοντας τῶν φυλῶν τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραὴλ, λέγων· Τοῦτο τὸ ῥῆμα ὃ συνέταξε Κύριος· Ἄνθρωπος ὃς ἂν εὔξηται εὐχὴν Κυρίῳ, ἢ ὀμόσῃ ὅρκον, ἢ ὁρισμῷ ὁρίσηται περὶ τῆς ψυχῆς αὐτοῦ, οὐ βεβηλώσει τὸ ῥῆμα αὐτοῦ. Πάντα ὅσα ἐξέλθῃ ἐκ τοῦ στόματος αὐτοῦ ποιήσει. Ἐὰν δὲ εὔξηται γυνὴ εὐχὴν Κυρίῳ, ἢ ὁρίσηται ὁρισμὸν ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτῆς ἐν τῇ νεότητι αὐτῆς, καὶ ἀκούσῃ ὁ πατὴρ αὐτῆς τὰς εὐχὰς αὐτῆς, καὶ τοὺς ὁρισμοὺς αὐτῆς οὓς ὡρίσατο κατὰ τῆς ψυχῆς αὐτῆς, καὶ παρασιωπήσῃ ὁ πατὴρ αὐτῆς· καὶ στήσονται πᾶσαι αἱ εὐχαὶ αὐτῆς, καὶ πάντες οἱ ὁρισμοὶ αὐτῆς οὓς ὡρίσατο κατὰ τῆς ψυχῆς αὐτῆς, μενοῦσιν αὐτῇ. Ἐὰν δὲ ἀνανεύων ἀνανεύσῃ ὁ πατὴρ αὐτῆς, ᾗ ἂν ἡμέρᾳ ἀκούσῃ πάσας τὰς εὐχὰς αὐτῆς, καὶ τοὺς ὁρισμοὺς αὐτῆς, οὓς ὡρίσατο κατὰ τῆς ψυχῆς αὐτῆς, οὐ στήσονται, καὶ Κύριος καθαριεῖ αὐτὴν, ὅτι ἀνένευσεν ὁ πατὴρ αὐτῆς.» Ἀλλ' εἰ καὶ γένοιτο, φησὶν, γυνὴ συνηρμοσμένη κατὰ νόμους ἀνδρὶ, ὁ αὐτὸς κρατείτω νόμος. Χήρας δὲ καὶ ἐκβεβλημένης ἵστησι τοὺς ὁρισμοὺς, καὶ διαπεραίνεσθαι δεῖν πάντη τε καὶ πάντως τὰς ὑποσχέσεις εὖ μάλα φησὶ, πανταχῆ τὸ ἐλεύθερον καὶ ἔξω ζυγοῦ ταῖς αἰτίαις ὑποτιθεὶς, εἰ μὴ δρᾷν ἕλοιτο τὰ ἐπηγγελμένα· τόγε μὴν οὐχ ὧδε ἔχον, ἄπρακτόν τε καὶ ὑφ' ἑτέροις, ἀνιεὶς εἰκότως. Τοῖς γάρτοι κυρίοις, πατρί τε, φημὶ, καὶ ἀνδρὶ, συνθεμένοις μὲν καὶ οἱονεὶ συννεύσασι
pass_a_gloss: [Continuation of §26:] ... not having the raw (ὠμός) and the hated (ἀπεχθάνομαι). You learned thoroughly (διαπυνθάνομαι) somewhere the [one] in purities (ἁγνεία) toward (ἐπί) the saving (σωτήριος) food (τροφή), as Christ naming [it] his own (ἴδιος) and saying to the holy disciples: 'I have food (βρῶσις) to eat which you do not know' [Jn 4:32]. Remember (διαμιμνήσκομαι) that he also ordered the lamb (ἀμνός) to be sacrificed (καταθύω) for a type of Christ, and further legislated (προσνομοθετέω) saying: 'You shall not eat from them raw, nor boiled (ἕψω) in water, but only roasted (ὀπτός) with fire' [Exod 12:9]; calling raw, I think, the unacceptable (ἀπαράδεκτος) and the as-it-were not easy (εὐχερής) for digestion (πέψις). Therefore he says the arm must be taken boiled; the unboiled (ἄνεφθος) signifying the neither sweet nor edible (βρώσιμος), and thus unacceptable. PALL.: How exceedingly subtle (ἰσχνός) and true the argument (λόγος). CYR.: So the professions/promises (ὁμολογία) must be rendered (ἀποδίδωμι) to God, and whatever one should vow (εὔχομαι), let him accomplish (διαπεραίνω) delaying (μέλλω) nothing; since the not doing such things swiftly (γοργῶς) I would call among the most dreadful (δεινός) and most dangerous (σφαλερός), and [so does] the sacred Writing (Γράμμα) itself. For if, thinking rightly, we reckon among the most outlandish (ἐκτοπώτατος) to be convicted (ἁλίσκομαι) by an indictment (γραφή) for false speaking (ψευδοέπεια), how would it not be among the very shameful (αἰσχρός) to profess and promise (ὑπισχνέομαι) something to God, and after this to falsify (ψεύδομαι) the promise (ὑπόσχεσις)? So of everyone who vowed and delayed, and indeed altogether shrank back from (ἀναδύομαι) the payment (ἔκτισις), he records (καταγράφω) the sin (ἁμαρτία). But he releases (ἀνίημι) from the charges (αἰτίαμα) those having nothing at all of their own, but yoked (καταζεύγνυμι) as by a necessary (ἀναγκαῖος) bond (δεσμός), and acting (πράττω) under another's hand (χείρ). It is written thus in Numbers: [Num 30:1-5 Eng = LXX 30:2-6] 'And Moses spoke to the rulers (ἄρχων) of the tribes (φυλή) of the sons of Israel saying: This is the word (ῥῆμα) which the Lord commanded (συντάσσω): A man who vows a vow (εὐχή) to the Lord, or swears (ὄμνυμι) an oath (ὅρκος), or defines with a definition/binding (ὁρισμῷ ὁρίζω) concerning his soul (ψυχή), shall not profane (βεβηλόω) his word; all that comes out of his mouth he shall do. If a woman vows a vow to the Lord, or defines a binding in her father's house in her youth (νεότης), and her father hears her vows and her bindings which she bound against her soul, and her father keeps silent (παρασιωπάω), all her vows shall stand (ἵστημι), and all her bindings ... shall remain (μένω) to her. But if her father, refusing, refuses (ἀνανεύω) on whatever day he hears all her vows and bindings ..., they shall not stand, and the Lord will cleanse (καθαρίζω) her, because her father refused.' But even if, he says, a woman were joined (συναρμόζω) lawfully to a husband, let the same law prevail (κρατέω) [Num 30:6-8]. Of a widow (χήρα) and a cast-out woman (ἐκβάλλω) he sets the bindings standing [Num 30:9], and says very well that the promises must be carried out in every way and by all means, everywhere putting the free (ἐλεύθερος) and outside the yoke (ζυγός) under the charges, if she should not choose (αἱρέομαι) to do the things announced (ἐπαγγέλλομαι); but the one not so placed, unable to act (ἄπρακτος) and under others, releasing fittingly. For to the masters (κύριος), father, I mean, and husband, having agreed (συντίθημι) and as it were having nodded assent (συννεύω) [continues in §28]
pass_b_english: Cyril: …with nothing raw or distasteful about them. You have learned, I think, that the one who lives in purity serves as saving food, food that Christ, as it were, calls his own when he says to the holy disciples: ‘I have food to eat that you do not know’ (John 4:32). Remember too that he commanded the lamb to be slaughtered as a type of Christ (Exodus 12:6), and laid down a further law, saying: ‘You shall not eat any of it raw, nor boiled in water, but only roasted with fire’ (Exodus 12:9). By ‘raw’ he means, I think, what is unacceptable and, as it were, hard to digest. So he says that the arm must be taken boiled, since what is uncooked signifies what is neither sweet nor fit to eat, and therefore unacceptable.
Palladius: How very subtle, and how true, the argument is!

Cyril: So we must pay to God what we have promised, and whatever anyone vows, let him carry it out without delay. For I would count failing to do such things promptly among the most dreadful and dangerous of faults, and so does sacred Scripture itself. If, thinking rightly, we reckon it among the most outrageous things to be convicted on a charge of lying, how would it not be utterly shameful to pledge something and promise it to God, and afterwards to prove false to that promise? So whenever anyone has vowed and then delayed, or has even shrunk back from paying altogether, the law records it against him as sin (Deuteronomy 23:21). But it releases from the charge those who have nothing at all of their own, but are yoked as by a binding necessity and act under another’s hand. It is written thus in Numbers: ‘And Moses spoke to the rulers of the tribes of the sons of Israel, saying: This is the word that the Lord has commanded. Any man who vows a vow to the Lord, or swears an oath, or binds himself with a pledge, shall not profane his word; he shall do all that comes out of his mouth. And if a woman vows a vow to the Lord, or binds herself with a pledge in her father’s house in her youth, and her father hears her vows and the pledges with which she has bound herself, and her father keeps silent, then all her vows shall stand, and all the pledges with which she has bound herself shall remain binding on her. But if her father firmly forbids it on the day he hears all her vows and her pledges with which she has bound herself, they shall not stand, and the Lord will cleanse her, because her father forbade it’ (Numbers 30:1–5). And even if, it says, the woman is lawfully married to a husband, the same law is to hold (Numbers 30:6–8). For a widow, however, and for a divorced woman, he lets the pledges stand (Numbers 30:9), and says, very rightly, that the promises must be carried out in every way and by all means. Everywhere he holds anyone who is free and outside the yoke liable to blame, if they will not choose to do what they promised; but anyone not so placed, who has no power to act and lives under others, he rightly releases. For against the masters, I mean the father and the husband, if they have agreed and, as it were, nodded assent…

Διεπύθου δέ που τὸν ἐν ἁγνείαις ἐπὶ τὴν σωτήριον τροφήν has no stated verb for τόν. Read as 'the one who lives in purity serves as saving food'; 'what is said of the one in purity concerning the saving food' is also possible. Open.

Opens with the end of the §26 sentence ('τὸ | ὠμὸν οὐκ ἔχοντα καὶ ἀπηχθημένον'), so the section opens 'Cyril: …'. Doubtful syntax: 'Διεπύθου δέ που τὸν ἐν ἁγνείαις ἐπὶ τὴν σωτήριον τροφήν' has no expressed verb for τόν; ἐπί + accusative is read here as 'serves as' ('the one who lives in purity serves as saving food, food that Christ calls his own'), following John 4:34–36, where Christ's food is doing the Father's will and gathering the harvest; the sense, from John 4:32–34, is that a pure life is food Christ calls his own. τόν could also stand for an understood λόγον; the reading is uncertain. Exodus 12:6 cited for the command to slaughter the lamb (a clear reference, not a quotation); Exodus 12:9 quoted from the LXX. Deuteronomy 23:21 (English) = Deuteronomy 23:22 (LXX/Hebrew) is the Scripture behind 'records it against him as sin'; Ecclesiastes 5:4–5 ('do not delay to pay it') is a further possible echo of 'without delay', left uncited. Numbers 30 numbering: Cyril's quotation is LXX/Hebrew Numbers 30:2–6 = English Numbers 30:1–5; the married-woman summary is English 30:6–8 (LXX 30:7–9); widow and divorced woman English 30:9 (LXX 30:10). ὁρισμός rendered 'pledge' (a binding obligation); 'περὶ/κατὰ τῆς ψυχῆς' rendered 'himself/herself' (Hebraism). καθαριεῖ kept as 'will cleanse her' (LXX for 'will forgive her'). ἐκβεβλημένη rendered 'divorced woman'. ψευδοεπείας ἁλῶναι γραφῇ is legal language (convicted on an indictment for lying). The section ends mid-sentence; the main verb ('he brings the charge of impiety') falls in §28.
